To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Fas is expressed in nontransformed breast cells, but is not expressed in most breast cancer cells, and that the Fas pathway can be reconstituted by transfection of the ICE gene in breast cancer cells.
the Fas pathway is important in the control of apoptosis in normal breast epithelial cells and is down-regulated in breast cancer cells.
the expression and function of the apoptotic Fas pathway is altered during breast cancer progression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of tumor progression and apoptosis, which are two important aspects of the pathogenesis of breast cancer.
understanding how the immune system controls the growth of normal breast epithelial cells and the development of breast cancer.
the role of apoptosis in breast cancer progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the down-regulation of the Fas pathway may play a role in breast cancer progression, and that reconstitution of Fas expression or function may provide an approach for inducing apoptosis in breast tumors.
the expression of Fas is not a prerequisite for the induction of apoptosis by Fas ligand in the breast cancer cells.

the expression and function of the death receptors and their pathways are complex and variable in normal and malignant cells and that further studies are needed to understand their role in normal and neoplastic breast epithelial cells and their regulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Fas is expressed and functional in normal human mammary epithelial cells and in the breast cancer cell line T47D but not in most other breast cancer cell lines.
Fas expression and function is down-regulated during the progression of breast cancer.
the Fas-mediated apoptotic pathway in normal mammary epithelial cells is intact and functional.
The main takeaway from our work is that
breast cancer cells are resistant to Fas induced apoptosis.
Fas expression is down-regulated during tumor progression and that this may be an important step in the development of breast cancer.
Fas expression is downregulated in breast cancer cells compared with normal mammary cells, and Fas sensitivity can be induced in these breast cancer cells by cytokines such as interferon.
